[b]Expansion into the South[/b]
[sub]A Sikirsk Expansion Post.[/sub]]

[b]Sikirskian Expansion Post - Northern West Shamat Colonization[/b]

Dateline: May 15, 2025

From: Office of External Settlements and Strategic Development, Central Planning Directorate

The Grand Federation of Sikirsk has formally initiated Phase I of its southern colonial expansion effort into the region historically referred to as the "Northern West Shamat Wasteland." Contrary to previous assumptions in northern Sikirsk, the region is not desolate, icy, or lifeless. Instead, settlers and accompanying defence personnel report strikingly hot and arid climates, punctuated by dry savannas, stretches of desert basins, and scattered groves of resilient trees native to the interior.

The first wave of state-guided settlers, accompanied by two regiments from the 4th Mechanized Infantry Division, landed on the southern coastal ridge known by its local name Kharins Reach. Their arrival, marked by the hoisting of the Sikirskian standard and the establishment of Forward Outpost 14-V, was carried out without incident.

Reports from Colonel Atrov Murn, commanding officer of the security detachment, describe the landing conditions as harsh but manageable. Winds reaching from inland heat fronts created difficulty during the unloading of supply vessels, but engineering teams were quick to lay down reinforced modular roads for armoured transport and water filtration systems.

The temperature during landing reached 28°C under full sun, a stark contrast to the often near-zero tempratures back in the Sikirskian islands. Many of the deployed Sikirskian personnel, equipped with climate-adapted fatigues and high-output hydration kits, reported the transition to be physically demanding, though morale remained high. "It feels like stepping into an oven." one soldier reportedly joked. The terrain, described by the colonists as "shifting between dust and green strips of savanna," is regarded as having long-term agricultural potential if irrigation is properly managed.

Reconnaissance efforts revealed no significant signs of preexisting large-scale human habitation. A few structures of unknown origin likely tribal or pre-wasteland shelters were sighted inland but appeared to be long-abandoned. A single encounter was recorded between a scouting unit inside a Sikirskian APC and a pair of desert wanderers on foot. The situation was resolved peacefully, with field translators establishing basic contact. The individuals appeared startled but not hostile and quickly withdrew after minor barter and observation. No further signs of concentrated resistance or formal claims to the land have been found thus far.

To solidify its presence, Sikirsk has begun construction of what will become the first permanent southern colonial hub: Velkarin Base. Designed to serve both military and civilian purposes, Velkarin will feature concrete housing units, solar-fed water processing plants, regional command offices, and a civilian administrative centre. The buildout will unfold over three stages across the next 4 months, according to planners.

The Central Planning Directorate has already mapped resource zones for future exploitation, with satellite imagery showing promising mineral deposits and subterranean aquifers. Additionally, biological survey teams from the Sikirskian Academy of Natural Sciences have deployed to investigate unique plant and animal life native to the region, with potential applications in medicine, food security, and industrial use.

Efforts are also being made to encourage controlled migration from inner Sikirsk toward the colony. Civilian families who volunteer for the first 200 settlements will receive special compensation, including land rights, elevated citizen status, and direct government support for farming and trade initiatives.

Colonial patrols continue to expand the safe perimeter around Velkarin, with plans to link the growing hub to future inland outposts via rail and convoys. Despite the challenges of the terrain, including the ever-present heat, sandstorms, and sudden wildlife activity, the Sikirskian spirit of discipline and order holds strong.

The international reaction to the colonization campaign has been cautious but observant. Several neutral nations have released brief statements requesting transparency and urging environmental oversight. Notably, the factionalized nation of Sal-Baliz, often regarded with suspicion due to its internationally condemned "activities", issued an unexpectedly supportive comment. While most governments remain diplomatically reserved, analysts agree that the eyes of the continent are now firmly turned toward the unfolding developments in Northern West Shamat.

[/spoiler]

[spoiler=
[b]Civilian Beginnings in Velkarin Base[/b]
[sub]A more inside look on the base.[/sub]]

As the first wave of settlers began to unpack crates, pitch prefabricated shelters, and erect satellite dishes under the harsh Southern sun, the civilian chapter of Sikirsks expansion into the Northern West Shamat Wasteland quietly began. Though overshadowed in official bulletins by the militarys role and strategic value of the region, life within the slowly rising Velkarin Base is already forming a unique civilian rhythmmarked by heat, labor, hope, and the frontier spirit that many Sikirskian families have long romanticized.

The base, still only partially complete, serves both military and civilian purposes, and thus gives rise to a daily dynamic unlike anything in the urban sectors of northern Sikirsk. Civilian quarters are grouped along the southern edge of the zone, in rows of hard-plated modular housing that shimmer under the desert sun. These structuresinitially intended for use in permafrost zoneshave been retrofitted with wide ventilation ducts, solar paneled awnings, and thermal shutters to combat the blazing heat of midday.

Each family unit is provided with a basic but functional living space: two insulated rooms, a solar-powered food unit, emergency communication computer, and access to a shared water node and shade area. For many of the settlers, its wierdbut clean, safe, and promising. Most are younger couples, farmers, engineers, or technical staff chosen from volunteer lists back home. Their presence is deliberate: to establish the foundation of a functioning civic environment while Velkarin matures from an outpost into a real town.

Civilian life here follows a strict timetable. Work crews, made up of a mix of conscripted laborers, tradespeople, and trained engineers, begin at dawn. Dust is swept aside before the sun fully rises, with tasks ranging from building roads and irrigation lines to assembling schools and small market depots. Meanwhile, supply drops arrive by cargo landers twice a week, watched with great interest by children and adults alike. Food remains mostly importednutrient packs, canned proteins, and root vegetablesthough pilot agricultural plots are being tested by soil teams just outside the perimeter.

Education and culture are also priorities, even in these early days. The first temporary learning hallmade from reinforced shipping containershas opened for settlers children, run by three assigned teachers from the mainland. The curriculum includes basic language, arithmetic, and environmental awareness focused on the new region's ecology. Already, a wall inside the hall displays childrens paintings: green trees growing from red sand, Sikirskian flags beside vast hills, imagined creatures of the Southern desert.

Social gatherings are small but meaningful. Evenings, once temperatures cool, often see civilians congregating near the central generator hub, where a community board has been established. Here, announcements are posted, radio messages played, and once weekly, a projector screen shows older Sikirskian films or documentaries under the stars. It's become tradition for settlers to bring small items to sharedried fruit, written poems, or carved wooden animals.

Security is omnipresent but not overbearing. Patrols pass through the civilian zones at regular intervals, and strict curfews are enforced after sundown. However, there is a noted effort to maintain a sense of autonomy for civilian life, with the base commander encouraging the formation of local committees to oversee neighborhood decisions. A Velkarin Civic Initiative has already been formed, and its representatives are currently coordinating a basic trade post and requesting additional recreational materials from the mainland.

The Future is bright. (You know, like the sun, lol)
[/spoiler]

[b]THEP SPACE AGENCY - HYDRONIA OFFICES
9:12am HST+7[/b]

A middle-aged Thrømm satellite operator sits at his desk, as usual. Nothing out of the ordinary has happened today, or yesterday, or in fact for the past year of his life. That was until 9:12am today. As he stares into the lifeless image from above Hydronia, he sees something odd. A group of around 35 ships, possibly more speeding through the eastern strait. He rubs his eyes just to make sure he isnt hallucinating, but the ships stay on the screen, moving towards the Hydronian coast pixel by pixel.
Sir, you might want to take a look at this, he shouts across the room in his Elysran accent. A stern looking Hydronian gets out from behind a desk and strolls over, sipping his morning coffee. The Thrømm points out the small specks of the ships, the zooms in.
[i]*SPPPPPP*[/i]
The Hydronian spits his coffee all over the screen.
What the K*hretsin[i](Hydronian for f*ck)[/i]! Get me contact with the base, NOW! He shouts. The Thrømm begins to dial in a number to call the nearby military base, Tursan 5, as everyone in the office crowds around the screen, with looks of panic
